idiom_name: DAO class over ADO.NET DbConnection/DbCommand (EF Core DbContext as the ORM alternative)
implementation_notes: C# puts the whole driver layer in the base class library, so the DAO is a small class rather than a subsystem: inject an IDbConnection (or a connection factory) plus a DbContext where the domain is ORM-mapped, execute with DbCommand.ExecuteReader/SqlCommand and project SqlDataReader rows into transfer objects, or let a micro-ORM such as Dapper perform the mapping. What replaces the classic structure is the framework: ADO.NET supplies connection pooling, commands, parameters and readers, while EF Core supplies DbSet/DbContext as a ready-made gateway for a mapped domain. The hand-written DAO is still justified for non-relational or legacy stores, for reporting paths where explicit SQL matters, and when part of the application must stay independent of the ORM.
pitfalls: SqlDataReader is a live, forward-only cursor bound to its connection: materialise the row before returning, and never let a DataReader or DbConnection leave the DAO.

Disposal is mandatory - a leaked ADO.NET connection is only reclaimed when the pool is exhausted, so the symptom appears much later as a timeout; also remember ExecuteReader requires an open connection.
Catching SqlException or EF Core's DbUpdateException in business code re-couples callers to the store; translate to an application exception type inside the implementation.
